name: Treaty at Camp Fremont, near the little Mariposa River (1851), unratified California treaty M
aka: Treaty M of the eighteen unratified California treaties of 1851-1852
citation: Never ratified; printed by order of the Senate, January 19, 1905
promises: Article 3 or 4 set apart a defined tract 'forever' for the occupancy of the signing tribes, here the district between the Merced and Tuolumne rivers, 'supposed to contain about four full townships'.
Beef cattle and flour for subsistence during 1851 and 1852.
Livestock, ploughs, tools, seed, iron and steel, blankets and clothing, divided by the tribes' numbers.
A farmer, a blacksmith, a carpenter and school teachers, with a school house, for at least five years.

breaches.what: This treaty (treaty M in the President's schedule) was one of eighteen made with California Indians in 1851-52 that the Senate refused to ratify in executive session on July 8, 1852, and placed under an injunction of secrecy that was removed only on January 18, 1905.
breaches.whoFoundIt: United States Senate, executive session; record reprinted 1905

source.title: Robert F. Heizer, The Eighteen Unratified Treaties of 1851-1852 between the California Indians and the United States Government (1972)
source.publisher: Archaeological Research Facility, University of California, Berkeley

breaches.what: Congress let the Indians of California sue for lands the United States took without compensation, and declared their loss from failing to secure the lands and compensation in the eighteen unratified treaties sufficient ground for equitable relief.

source.title: Act of May 18, 1928, ch. 624, 45 Stat. 602 (Indians of California jurisdictional act)

breaches.quote: the loss to the said Indians on account of their failure to secure the lands and compensation provided for in the eighteen unratified treaties

breaches.what: The Southern Sierra Miwuk Nation states that the tracts its ancestors reserved in the 1851-52 treaties, in exchange for ceding large areas of their homeland, were never confirmed or set aside for them and that the federal government's promises were never fulfilled after the Senate, under pressure from California's senators, refused ratification.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Southern Sierra Miwuk Nation, The Southern Sierra Miwuk Nation: A Compelling Case for Federal Recognition (narrative published on its website)

source.title: The Southern Sierra Miwuk Nation: A Compelling Case for Federal Recognition

landTaken: The tribes' lands in California, taken without the reserved tract or compensation; Royce areas 273, 274 mark the cession and the intended reservation.
compensation: Under the Act of May 18, 1928 the Court of Claims could award the value of the lands and compensation proposed in the eighteen treaties, with land at $1.25 an acre, less offsets. The amount finally paid was not located in this pass.
today: The treaty remains unratified. The National Archives' 2013 account describes the rejection as leaving most California Indians without land.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation says the United States made the 1851-52 treaties with the Southern Sierra Miwuk and their neighbors to end the Mariposa War waged by state-funded militias, that its ancestors ceded large areas of homeland while reserving tracts the United States promised to protect, that those lands were never set aside and the promises never kept, and that most of its people were left landless.

openQuestions: The Senate never ratified this treaty, so its promises never bound the United States; it is shown as never ratified. The 1928 Act is recorded as the government's own acknowledgment of the loss.
One record covers the whole set of eighteen treaties for the facts common to all; the other seventeen are the cession-1851-* and cession-1852-* entries for Royce areas 273 to 310.

The tribal names are as the commissioners wrote them in 1851-52; most are village or local group names, not nations, and how each community names itself today was not established. treaties.json lists as present-day tribes: California Valley Miwok Tribe, California; Ione Band of Miwok Indians of California; Picayune Rancheria of Chukchansi Indians of California; Santa Rosa Indian Community of the Santa Rosa Rancheria, California; Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, Shingle Springs Rancheria (Verona Tract), California; Table Mountain Rancheria of California.

The Court of Claims judgment under the 1928 Act (Indians of California v. United States, 98 Ct. Cl. 583, 1942) and the Indian Claims Commission settlement for the Indians of California (Dockets 31 and 37) were not opened in this pass; they are the leads for the amounts paid.

Article 2 of the treaties had the tribes relinquish all their lands in California; because the Senate rejected the treaties, the United States took the land without the reserved tracts or the promised goods (1928 Act, section 2).
